utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, will you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, The Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Tecla Benjamin, Ekkehard Withopf, and Ruth Karper, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. And now the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, lead counsel; Stefane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Mirna Milanovic, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, Rodney Dixon, and Mr. Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber bids good afternoon to all staff present, representatives of the OTP, the attorneys for the accused, the accused, and all the staff members, Mr. Registrar, Madam Usher, the court reporters, and I don't wish to forget the interpreters in the booth and the technical staff. On our programme for today, we have two witnesses planned, and without further ado, I should like to ask Madam Usher to go and fetch the first witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Are you hearing a translation of my words in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called to appear as a Prosecution witness. To do that, you have to take the solemn declaration. But before that, I need to identify you by asking you some questions. First of all, give me your first and last name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ivo Kolenda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1940, on the 6th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Cukle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am now retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in 1993, what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, I had already retired then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you ever testified in court, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never testified before. This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you're testifying on behalf of the Prosecution, you need to take the solemn declaration by reading the text that Madam Usher is going to hand to you. So please read the text in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated. Before we begin with your testimony, I need to give you some information regarding the way in which these proceedings will develop, and especially your own testimony. You will be asked to answer questions that will be put to you by the representatives of the OTP, who are seated to your right. And I believe it is Madam Benjamin who will be asking questions, because she is behind the pulpit. Once you have answered all the questions that are going to be put to you by a representative of the Prosecution, the lawyers for the Defence, who are located to your left, there are six of them, and only one or two will be asking you questions, and they will do so in order to verify what you told the Prosecutor in answering their questions and to check your credibility, and also regarding the general context of events. The three Judges in front of you, should they deem it necessary, may, at any point in time, also ask you questions in order to clarify your answers. Sometimes the questions are complicated. If you don't understand them, ask the person putting them to you to rephrase them. If the question seems to you unclear or too complicated, please do not hesitate for the question to be repeated. As far as possible, try and answer fully and precisely, though you will be testifying about events that took place more than ten years ago. If you've forgotten, tell us so frankly. As you're testifying under oath, I need to tell you that you have pledged to tell the whole truth. Then you must not give any lies. Should you provide false testimony, you must know that you are exposing yourself to the possibility of being prosecuted and that the punishment for false testimony can be a fine and a prison sentence up to seven years. Also, when answering questions, if certain points could one day be taken against you, you may refuse to answer that question. In this very specific situation, the Chamber may force you to provide an answer, but even then, what you say cannot be taken against you one day in the future. I needed to explain all this so that you should realise the importance of your testimony. Without wasting any time, I turn to the Prosecution Bench, and I give the floor to Ms. Benjamin for the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Examined by Ms. Benjamin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kolenda, you indicated to the Trial Chamber that you were born in Cukle. Could you tell us in which municipality Cukle is situated.

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: In Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you give us a breakdown of the ethnic composition of Cukle, please.

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Before the war, there were Serbs, Muslims, and Croats, but now, since these events, there are only two ethnicities: Serbs and Croats [as interpreted]. There are no Serbs [sic] anymore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you state for the Trial Chamber if you are married and if you have children.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. Instead of Serbs, Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: I'm married. I have some children. One son was killed, so I now from six.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you ever a member of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us what period you served, please.

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Between '61 and 1963.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. In the transcript, in line -- on page 5 - I can't see the line - 7 and 8, it says that the witness said that there are only two ethnicities in the village: Serbs and Croats. But the witness actually said that there were two ethnicities: Muslims and Croats. So there's an error in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, he said that only Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Croats and Muslims were left, whereas line 7 of page 5 says that there were Serbs and Croats. So we wish to correct that line. Please continue, Madam Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you, Mr. Kolenda, state for the Trial Chamber the relationship that existed between the Muslims and Croats before the conflict in Cukle.

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Before the conflict started, relations between the Croats and Muslims were good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you emphasise for us when you say "good," what you mean.

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: We worked together, we visited each other. When we sent our children to the army, or when there were weddings, we would join in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kolenda, did there come a time when these relationships became strained?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes. They were aggravated when there was this hesitation, sometime around February and March. Things didn't work any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the commencement of June 1993, could you tell us what the atmosphere was like in Cukle, please.

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: It was hard. The situation was difficult. When the shooting started and when each village started guard duty, until then, there was confidence between them, but after that, things deteriorated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kolenda, could you kindly now state for the Trial Chamber or relate for the Trial Chamber the events of the 8th of June, 1993 as they unfolded.

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: On that day, the events started about 4.00 a.m. There was an attack from all sides on Cukle and Susanj and Grahovcici and Brajkovici. We were surrounded. There was gunfire from all sides. There were soldiers. First they broke through the lines at Mehurici, and they entered from that direction and they set fire to I think five houses, and this was before dawn. And when it dawned, they started shelling Grahovcici and the hill above it. And this went on until 9.00. Then the people of Cukle started withdrawing from Gornje Cukle towards Ovnak and Cekine Kuce. And this was going on until midday. And I said to my wife and my sister-in-law, who is older - she was born in 1937, and there were younger women. I said, "You must withdraw. We must take the children. We can't stay on here." And the women went first. I left later, about 12.00. And then there were a lot of soldiers from Orasac and Donje Cukle, and they protected us until darkness fell. A lot of people were killed. That was the day my son was killed, around 11.00, near the Babic houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kolenda --

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us at this point in time: Were your sons at home with you?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes. He was close to my house, and he was wounded in the right arm from a hunting rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which son would this have been?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Mijo. He was wounded there, around 9.00, behind the houses. A bullet was taken out of his arm. He went to the hospital, to Grahovcici. And after that, around 11.00, my son Petar was killed, who was born in 1971. We then withdrew, around 12.00. We went towards Grahovcici, but I don't know what really went on after that. The soldiers ordered that all civilians should withdraw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On your leaving the village of Cukle, could you tell the Court what you observed as you left the village. What did you see?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: When we climbed up near my house, I saw that some soldiers had arrived there, and they took out my horse and cows and there was maize and grass around. And then Marko said to me: "Look, they've let the animals out." And I said: "Let them." And then I went up the hill and I didn't see anything else. When we were withdrawing from Ceka's [phoen] house towards Pokrajcici, around 6.00, and it was already dark when we got to Pokrajcici, I saw houses burning, my brothers' houses, who were above mine. Stipe, Zorko's, and Fabijo's. That is where their houses and stables were. And they were set on fire that very night. As for the others, I went there the next day to carry food to the soldiers at Pjescara, and they had binoculars and I could see through them that every night they would set fire to one or two house and stables. And then when there was a ceasefire, I have a friend who stayed there during the war. There were people from Siprag, then Kotor Varos, and they had livestock and cows, and they had entered our houses. And then Rigici [phoen] came and set fire to all the stables. He said -- they said that it was all theirs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kolenda, could you assist us? When you say "they," what do you mean by "they"? They set fire to the houses, they took the horses. Whom do you refer to when you say "they"?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Soldiers. I suppose it was the 3rd Corps and the 7th Muslim Brigade. There were soldiers from all over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you specify the 3rd Corps and the 7th Muslim Brigade? Is there any reason that you suspected that these soldiers were from that unit?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: I think they were, because there were attempts to attack our forces at Usice and Grahovcici two or three times. Two soldiers were killed before this conflict, and they wanted to break through, and then they grouped themselves, and that is how it happened. And then when we got to Ceka's houses, there were so many soldiers at once. There were so many of them coming from all sides, from the mountain, soldiers from Zenica, from Han Bila. We were surrounded, you see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber what the village of Cukle looked like one week after the conflict.

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Everyone stayed in their houses. No one walked around. Nothing was destroyed or anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the houses look like in Cukle?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Before the conflict or after the conflict?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the conflict, the day after.

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: After the conflict. If you didn't see it, you wouldn't believe it. No roofs. No one has come back to the village to this day. There's Gornje Cukle. No one has come. Orasac, Miletici. No one has returned yet. All you can see are the bare walls, and they were all houses with two floors, or one and a half floors, before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What have your houses -- could you tell the Trial Chamber how it looked one week after the conflict?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: As far as I was able to see from Pjescara, when I was taking food for the soldiers and I was looking through binoculars, every night you could see cars driving off things from houses, and a house or two being set on fire. Until the ceasefire came. When the ceasefire came, I went down and I saw everything. We went there by bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the condition of your house when you saw it?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: When I arrived, I had two houses and stables, but everything was burnt down. The roofs had fallen in. One has been repaired. The other hasn't yet. That's how it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remain in Nova Bila after the conflict?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: I was in Stara Bila during the conflict. We were in a house and we were crowded, because refugees had come from all sides. There were six families, 28 of us in a single house. We had to lie down next to one another. We were crammed there. And then after this ceasefire, we went to -- I went to Pero Kalic's [phoen] house until my house was repaired. I applied to return first, and I returned immediately, as soon as I could. It will be five years now that I've gone back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So could you tell the Trial Chamber: Where do you live at present?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: I'm living in Cukle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, could you tell us: What is the relationship now between the Muslims and Croats in Cukle?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. The older ones are somehow managing to talk to one another. As to the younger ones, those in the 30s, they won't Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. even say hello to you. I had some problems when I returned. When the children were small, they were 2 or 3 years old, and now they're attending school. So I was -- they were 7 or 8 when I returned. And they say "Salamaleikum", and I kept quiet. And I stopped a child and asked him, "Is that what the teacher teaches you?" He didn't answer. And then a driver came from Alivodja [phoen], and I said this to him, and he went down there to their teacher and explained everything. And then they stopped teasing me and harassing me. Now the children are coming and going and saying good day normally. But I did have problems when I first returned. But things are okay now, thank God.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kolenda.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this is the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kolenda, I have a question for you which follows on from an answer that you gave. You said that there was an attack and that you asked your family members to leave your house after your son had been wounded in the arm. You said that there were soldiers. But what we don't know is whether you saw these soldiers. And if you did, how far away were they from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were about 500 metres from me. They were a little below the house and I was on a hill. We were observing what was happening. And it wasn't just from one side. If you know the lay of the land there, that's how it is. That's what I saw. They were coming from all sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had olive-drab uniforms, sir, on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that they were members of the 3rd Corps or of the 7th Muslim Brigade. On what basis have you made this claim? Is this an inference that you drew or was there any information that -- any elements that support your claim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't support what I have stated, but they can't just be from Cukle or from Mehurici. You can't have so many soldiers from those areas. They must have been preparing to have the inhabitants moved away from Cukle, Orasac, and Miletici, Maljine and Guca Gore and Grahovcici and Susanj and Brajkovici. One platoon can't liberate such an extensive territory in one day. This all took place in one day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that at the beginning you saw houses on fire as soon as the attack started. How were these houses set on fire? Yes. My question was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were three houses and two stables, and they were set on fire immediately up there. My brothers' houses. They were a little above mine, about 600 metres further up, up the hill from my house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you said that they were your brothers' houses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How were they set on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, how do I know? I wasn't in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you yourself saw them burning. Did you see them burning from the place where you were at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did. I saw them. Everything could be seen from where I was, Donje Cukle, Gornje Cukle, Ovnak. Everything can be seen. You just couldn't see Susanj and Koljevici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By the houses which were on fire, did you see any soldiers or was there no one there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no. You couldn't see that. It wasn't near.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll now turn to the Defence. Are there any questions that the Defence would like to put to the witness? But I'm sure there are. You may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have a few questions for Mr. Kolenda. Cross-examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, witness. Good day, Mr. Kolenda. My name is Edina Residovic and I represent General Hadzihasanovic. As the president of the Chamber has already told you, I'll be asking you a number of questions, and please answer them if you know the answers. If my question doesn't seem to be sufficiently precise, let me know and I will try to rephrase the question a little more clearly. Mr. Kolenda, you've said that you lived in Cukle, in Travnik municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, your house was in a part of Cukle called Novo Selo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Ovnak and Novo Selo and Cukle. We were near Cukle, and Grahovcici was near, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your village was a separate village from the village of Cukle, although it was part -- it belonged to that village of Cukle?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It was separate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Gornje Cukle, Muslims and Croats lived there before the war, likewise in your town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Muslim houses were in the middle, and the Croatian houses were on the outskirts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were other Croatian villages around your village, Ovnak, Susanj, and Grahovcici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and Orasac further up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your Novo Selo -- Ovnak was closest to Novo Selo, which was about two kilometres from the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: No. Ovnak is about 300 metres from my house. When the phone lines were introduced, they found out that it was exactly 300 metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, the other places, Grahovcici, are further away, five or six kilometres?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Two kilometres from my house. Grahovcici is two kilometres from my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the conflict, there was an HVO platoon in Donje Cukle, which was part of a company that had its command post in Grahovcici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About 20 people from Novo Selo were HVO members; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Well, not even 20. There were about ten of them. There weren't that many young men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning, these HVO members went together with army members to the lines on Mount Vlasic, facing the Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. My Petar was there too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, as you said in response to a question from my learned colleague, in February or March, the relationship between the HVO and army deteriorated, and after that, the members of the HVO didn't go to Vlasic; they held guard duty and fortified themselves around the village?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: No. They went there together, and when they returned, when they were returning from duty on one day, from Kajbasa [phoen], then at Zukica bridge they took their weapons and captured them. They confiscated the lorry and then a few hours later they let them go home without anything. My son came about 3.00, should have come about 10.00, and then the relationship deteriorated and they no longer went to the line together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in Ovnak, 300 metres away from your house, there was an HVO checkpoint; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes. There was a checkpoint there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the Jure Francetic Brigade in Zenica had been disarmed in the middle of April 1993, some of the soldiers from that brigade arrived in your area and became part of the brigade that your unit belonged to? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes. Part of them, but on the whole, they all escaped to Nova Bila at night. Only a few remained, about ten men from the Francetic unit remained. They would run away at night when they were sent to complete a task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As of that time, they started establishing fortified lines from Ovnak in the direction of Grahovcici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Opposite the checkpoint in Ovnak, through the checkpoint in Ovnak, people going from Zenica to Travnik weren't able to pass through very often, because the HVO would send them back at the checkpoint; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes. But they would also capture people in a checkpoint. You couldn't pass through. There were some young men who were captured. This is what I have stated. People were captured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning of June, eight buses with BH army members were captured. They were supposed to go to the defence line in Turbe. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes. They were sent back. I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Early in the morning on the 8th of June, you said that you heard shooting from the direction of Mehurici, Suhi Dol, and Zagrdje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These villages are quite far away from your village?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes, they are. But they went to Mrkonje from there, and the lines were right by Mrkonje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first lines that the HVO had were in fact at the exit from Cukle, in Mrkonje?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes, about 50 metres away, there was a line, and then there was the HVO line, the BH line, and the HVO line were close to each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that morning, in fact, in Cukle itself, the attack first started against Mrkonje and then these houses that you have mentioned were set on fire?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you were in your house, you didn't see how these houses were set on fire and you didn't see who did it?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I was -- it was two kilometres away from my house at least, so I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you said, you withdrew with some inhabitants in the direction of Ovnak?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Ovnak and Cekina Kuce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From Cekine Kuce, as you explained a little earlier on, you saw that some soldiers had taken a horse and cow out of your stable?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last thing you saw was that the horse and cow were grazing in the field, and then you moved away and you didn't see what happened afterwards?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some time in the afternoon, about 3.00 p.m., you set off in the direction of Pokrajcici, where there were lorries waiting for you. These lorries took all of you to Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Not about 3.00, but when night fell, there was a mine down there, and Han Bila was there. We couldn't go before. We were waiting, men, women, and children. We were waiting by Cekine Kuce until night fell and then we withdrew under cover of the night. It was about 10.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were waiting in Cekine Kuce, inhabitants from the village of Orasac also arrived. They were withdrawing, together with HVO members from the village of Orasac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes. From Donje Cukle, from Orasac, they were withdrawing. At about 9.00. They were -- the women and children who were withdrawing and the troops were providing protection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In response to a question put to you by the President of the Chamber, you said that you could see how your brothers' houses had burnt?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Two brothers of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You observed that after you had been assigned to carry water and food for the HVO to the lines in Pokrajcici?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: No. It was that night that the houses burnt down. But later I was given these tasks, and then there were another 12 houses and stables that burnt down. The names of the people are available. I have mentioned them. I had two houses, my brother Zorko had two houses and Stipo had two, Niko Baric had two houses, Vinko had a stable. There were 12 houses and 12 stables that burnt down after that. Every day you'd be told that there was another house burning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, you observed all of this from Pjescara, which is about seven or eight kilometres from your village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes. I think that that would be the distance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Everything that you could see from that distance during that month, all you could see was smoke?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not able to know how the houses were set on fire or who did it?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: No. But there were people who spoke about it. There were people from Kotor Varos and people who came from Ovnak. They said: "Your neighbour Ridja [phoen] didn't let us do anything. They set fire to the stables. When we returned, that man was up there with the sheep." Then he went to see my friend. He asked my friend: "What are you looking for?" He said: "I have some friends, Ivo and Marko, up in the field."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Everything you have just told me, things that you found out about a lot later?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes, a lot later, when the truth had been established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the truth that you have mentioned happened after the Washington Agreement, in 1994, and the first time you went to the village was in 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You returned to your village, to your house, in 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kolenda.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll now turn to the other Defence team. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. As Your Honours will be aware, Mr. Kubura is not charged in the indictment with any alleged incidents in connection with the village of Cukle, which is essentially what the witness has testified about today. And, Your Honours, we therefore have no questions for this witness on behalf of Mr. Kubura. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dixon. I'll turn to Mr. Withopf and Mrs.. Benjamin. Any other questions you would like to ask the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, I'll just ask the witness one question, please. Re-examined by Ms. Benjamin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, your house was in Novo Selo, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you had to leave the village, you were in Pokrajcici

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Grahovcici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The area that you took the food to the soldiers, what is that area?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Pokrajcici. Pokrajcici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court what is the distance between Pokrajcici and Novo Selo.

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Well, the distance is about eight kilometres, the distance between Pokrajcici and Novo Selo. If you use another route, the distance is not as great. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would I be correct in asking you if, from your vantage point in Pokrajcici, if you were able to see houses burning in Novo Selo?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Well, it's a hill. You could see the entire village, and Ovnak. It was very clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you see?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Well, you could see the houses burning in the evening. They didn't burn during the day. When we would take food to the people, then you could see two or three houses burning, until all the houses had been set on fire. They didn't set fire to some of the houses which were inhabited, but they did when people left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in fact you did see these houses burning probably a day or two days after the conflict; am I right?

utterances.speaker: IVO KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes. Two days afterwards or perhaps even more.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. This is all for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mrs. Benjamin. Mr. Kolenda, this concludes your testimony. The Prosecution has examined you, the Defence has also examined you, and the Judges have also asked you some questions to clarify certain matters. Thank you for having come to testify at The Hague, especially about events that are painful, given that you have told us that you lost your son in the course of these events.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I lost my son and in Pjescara, Josip was wounded. He was born in 1974. On the 12th of June is when it happened, three days later. He's disabled. He has only managed to start walking. There was a shell that hit the balcony. So I have two who are wounded. One was seriously wounded. One son was killed. But the other son was slightly wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber would like to thank you for having contributed to determining the truth. On behalf of the Judges, I wish you a good trip home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything I have said has been correct. I wouldn't have done otherwise. And I would like to thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll turn to the Prosecution now. Second witness has been scheduled for this hearing, Tomislav Mikulic is the name mentioned. Is that correct, Mr. Withopf?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President, and the witness is available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will wait for the usher to return. The usher has gone to fetch the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Let me check first that you can hear what I'm saying in your own language, thanks to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called as a 1 witness for the Prosecution to testify about events which took place in 1993, and within the framework of your testimony, and before you take your solemn declaration, I need to collect some information about you. So please, what is your first and last name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tomislav Mikulic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your date and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 28th of July, 1962, in Potkralj [phoen], municipality of Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your occupation or current activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a graduate mechanical engineer. Currently I'm working as a designer for central heating and air-conditioning systems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where are you residing at present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm living in Valpovo now, some 20 kilometres west of Osijek.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in 1993, what were you doing in terms of your professional activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a member of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you were a soldier or a civilian working for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a soldier. I was in charge of personnel in the battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified in court, or is this the first time in your life that you are testifying in court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my first appearance in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Within the framework of your testimony, you need to take a solemn declaration. For that purpose, please read the text on the card given to you by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated. Before giving the floor to the Prosecution for their examination-in-chief, I should like to provide some information for you, as I do for all witnesses, regarding the proceedings here, as this is your first time to testify in court, and you may be a bit confused by the surroundings. You have been called as a witness by the Prosecution, and you will have to answer questions that will be put to you in a moment by a representative of the Prosecution, who is behind the transparent plastic pulpit. The question that is going to be put to you, if they appear to be too complicated, you can ask the person asking you questions to rephrase them for you to be able to understand and answer them properly. The representative of the Prosecution is seated to your right. Once the Prosecution have completed their examination, the Defence counsel, who are seated to your left, will also have questions for you within the framework of a procedure known as the cross-examination. First, the examination-in-chief, and then the cross-examination. The questions will be put on the basis of the evidence that you provided, prompted by questions from the Prosecution, whereas the Defence will rely on the written statement that you signed when talking to the investigator of the OTP, and of course they will also rely on the questions put to you by the Prosecution. And they may also ask you some general questions. I also need to inform you that, as part of its defence duties, the lawyers certainly have conducted their own investigations into these events, and therefore, they may ask you questions that do not relate to what you stated in your written statement. Also, the three Judges in front of you may, whenever they consider it necessary, ask you questions to clarify any points that may appear hazy. As you have taken the solemn declaration to tell the whole truth and nothing but the truth, this, of course, means that you need to say everything and not to lie. Should you provide any false testimony at any point, you may be subject to prosecution for perjury, which is a serious offence and which is punished either by a fine or a prison sentence of up to seven years, or even both penalties at the same time. In view of the fact that you were a soldier in the HVO, it is possible, though of course the Chamber doesn't know what questions you will be asked, in the course of answering those questions, you might Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. possibly provide elements that may one day be taken against you. In that case, you can refuse to answer because you cannot incriminate yourself. Should that happen, the Chamber may ask you to answer those questions nevertheless, and in doing so, your replies cannot be used to incriminate you. You cannot be charged on that basis. And this is a very specific rule of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I thought it necessary to provide these explanations so that your testimony may be completed under the best possible conditions. Should you encounter any difficulty at all in the course of this hearing, please tell the Judges, who are in front of you. We have about 25 minutes before the break. Before any further ado, I give the floor to the Prosecution for their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours. Examined by Mr. Withopf:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mikulic.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulic, have you ever been a member of the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber from when to when.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: I served in the Yugoslav People's Army from the 8th of October, 1971 [as interpreted] to the 27th of August, 1972 [as interpreted]. For the first six months I was in the reserve officers' school in Bileca, until the 1st of April, 1982.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. It was '81 and '82.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: And then I was transferred to Zagreb, where I stayed until the end of my military service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you left the JNA in 1982, did you have a military rank?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: When I left the JNA, according to the rules of the reserve officers' school, one automatically received the rank of second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulic, where did you live in early 1993?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: In early 1993, I was in the unit permanently. I didn't go home at all. In Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And since when were you living in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: From the formation of the 2nd Battalion, that is, from the 4th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber about the ethnic composition of Bugojno in early 1993.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: In early 1993, the ethnic composition in relation to the situation at the beginning of the war was significantly changed with the arrival of numerous Bosniak refugees from Donji Vakuf in April 1992, about 12.000 of them, and again in October 1992, Bosniaks came from Jajce, so that the composition of the population was changed, and there was a significant majority of Bosniaks at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the situation about prior to the arrival of the refugees?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Before the beginning of the war, or rather, before the arrival of the refugees, roughly speaking, percentage-wise, about 41 per cent were Bosniaks, 36 per cent were Croats, and about 18 per cent were Serbs, and the rest were people who mostly declared themselves to be Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these person percentages, Mr. Mikulic, what does it mean in numbers of inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: There were close to 16.000 Croats. There were about 19 1/2 thousand Bosniaks, and Serbs, I think about 8.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, Mr. Mikulic, which ethnicity owned the majority of the land?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: It was the Croats who owned most of the land. According to official data, this percentage was about 68 per cent, the land owned by Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You already informed, Mr. Mikulic, the Trial Chamber that in 1993 you became a member of the HVO. Can you please tell us which unit of the HVO in Bugojno you did join.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: I became a member of the 2nd Battalion from the moment it was formed, of the 104th Brigade of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 104th Brigade of the HVO, did it have a second name, an additional name?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did. It was named after Eugen Kvaternik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were your duties, Mr. Mikulic?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: At first, I said that I was a personnel officer in the battalion, so I kept a record of soldiers who joined or who moved on to other units. So I had to delete them from the list. I issued certificates for people going to Croatia, mostly soldiers who went to visit their families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fulfilling your duties you just described, were you ever involved in any combat operations?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: I participated in combat operations only during the last couple of days of the conflict between the BH army and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please be a bit more concrete in respect to the last couple of days. Do you recall the exact dates?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: The conflicts officially between the BH army and the HVO in Bugojno started on the 18th of July, in the early hours of the morning, about 4.00 or 5.00 a.m., and they lasted until the 25th of July. And the last unit to surrender was our own unit, the 2nd Battalion, and this was about 7.30 or 8.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than the 2nd Battalion of the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade in Bugojno, were there any other military units?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: In Bugojno, there was a brigade consisting of three battalions. There were also some independent platoons, and these were mostly set up by individuals who had their own armies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the ABiH have military units in Bugojno in early 1993?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: In early 1993, the BH army was developed from the Territorial Defence, and after that, it became officially known as the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to your recollection, which brigade, if any, was located in Bugojno? Which ABiH brigade?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: The 307th Motorised Brigade was in Bugojno, but they too had some independent units, about which I cannot say with certainty who their commanders were, nor how exactly they were called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, who was the commander of the 307th ABiH Brigade in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Before the conflict with the HVO, the commander was Mr. Tahir Granic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And later on?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: And later on, he was succeeded by Faruk Aganovic. I'm not quite sure whether it was Beganovic or Aganovic, but I think it was Aganovic, known as Jupi, and he worked as a doorman in a department store before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You earlier on today, Mr. Mikulic, mentioned that in early 1993, thousands of Muslim refugees came to Bugojno. Amongst the Muslim refugees, were there men in a military age?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Of course there were men of military age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, did these men of military age amongst the Muslim refugees, did they join the 307th Brigade in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: They joined the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, probably the 307th Brigade, because as far as I know, there was no other brigade. And a smaller number of them joined the HVO. People had been left without their homes, and they had to look for some source of income, to receive some sort of a salary and to provide food for themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The smaller number of the refugees, of the Muslim refugees who joined the HVO, did they stay with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Most of them, at the end of March, left the HVO. They had to join the BH army, because conflicts had already started in other towns around Bugojno, so they couldn't stay in the HVO. Not that they were thrown out, but they themselves wanted to leave. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of numbers, which was the bigger army in the area of Bugojno: The HVO or the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: The ratio was certainly 5:1 in favour of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, if not even greater than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Earlier on, Mr. Mikulic, you mentioned the outbreak of the conflict between the HVO and the ABiH in Bugojno and that you were involved at this late stage in supporting the combat operations of the HVO. Did there come a time during this conflict when you were captured?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: On the 25th of July, when we learnt, over Radio Zagreb, a reporter in the news programme at 5.00, Vesna Koric, was reporting, and she said that the whole town was under the control of the BH army, that the only fighting going on was around the 2nd Battalion. I can say that a couple of days prior to this, representatives of BH army had called us to surrender, but we didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you surrender on the 25th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. The entire unit that happened to be there, but mostly it was the command and the guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself surrender?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To whom did you surrender?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Representatives of the BH army, that is, to soldiers of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And soldiers of which military unit of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Soldiers of the 307th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you surrendered, where were you brought to, if anywhere?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Nearby was the headquarters of the BH army and the Stipo Djerek elementary school, so they were taken to that elementary school, to the gym there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you please inform the Trial Chamber what happened to you and the other ones who surrendered in the school Stipo Djerek.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Before we arrived at the Stipo Djerek school, a soldier from a neighbouring village, whom I knew - that is, his face; I didn't know his name exactly - he took away my glasses, my pocket knife, and the photograph of my two-year-old daughter, and said he wouldn't return them to me. When we reached the gym, we had to lie face down on the ground, and then came the beatings, mostly with boots on our heads and backs. Watches and rings were taken off, the soldiers. I had the good fortune to keep, somehow - I don't know how - my wedding ring. It was left on my hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulic, were you yourself beaten?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: We didn't dare look around much, especially when we had to lie on the ground with our foreheads on the ground. What we could see was that they were soldiers of the BH army and members of the 307th Brigade. I can say that in that noise and chaos, three women were particularly prominent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these women also members of the 307th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: They were wearing military uniforms, and it was already dusk, so I was unable to see the insignia, nor was I close enough to be able to see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The valuables which were taken away, did you and the other soldiers, to your knowledge, were they given back to you?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: I think they weren't, because no one officially could have registered these valuables on behalf of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Stipo Djerek school, were you and the other HVO soldiers allowed to keep your uniforms?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: I kept my uniform, but my jacket was taken from me. However, later, when we entered the gym in the grammar school, I noticed that several of our soldiers were just wearing their underwear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The soldiers you've seen later on in the elementary school wearing nothing but their underwear, were they amongst the ones which were held captured in the Stipo Djerek school?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know three specific names of men, because we were together in the same unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please provide us with the names.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Ivica Sisto, Ivica Klepic and Ivo Barnjak. Ivo Barnjak and Ivica Klepic had their heads wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The wounds on the heads of these soldiers, were they a result, to your knowledge, of the beatings inflicted on them?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: I know that they were beaten in the Stipo Djerek school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen it yourself?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: No. I couldn't see anyone, because, as I was saying, we were lying face down on the ground. But I do know that while we were surrendering, when we had gathered there, they hadn't been wounded or injured before we came to the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long, Mr. Mikulic, were you and the other soldiers kept in the Stipo Djerek school?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Between one and a half and two hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After these one and a half to two hours, where were you brought to?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: After that, we were taken to Mahmut Busatlija grammar school. This is a distance of about two kilometres, which we covered running, with our hands behind our heads. We had to sing songs about the HVO and cry out, "Allahu Ekber." Passing by the soldiers, or rather, those that escorted us, some were beaten, mostly with rifle butts in the back, and I was one of those beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who brought you from the Stipo Djerek school to the Mahmut Busatlija school?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: It was between 2100 and 2130 hours. We couldn't really look, but we were taken there by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Whether the military police had come by then, we couldn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, if I may suggest to have the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. It is a quarter to 4.00. We are going to have a 25-minute break and we will resume work at 10 past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, you may take the floor again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulic, once you arrived at the Mahmut Busatlija school, where were you brought to?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: When we arrived there, when we arrived where we were taken to -- I'm not quite sure I've understood the question. We were taken into the Mahmut Busatlija school. Is that what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where to within the Busatlija school?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: When we arrived in the Mahmut Busatlija school, we were taken into the sports hall. As soon as we entered, the BH army soldiers formed a gauntlet and we were beaten on the back. We entered the sports hall. It was dark. Our hands were behind our heads. Then one of the commanders entered. I think he had the highest rank, or perhaps he was second in rank in the BH army command, Nijaz Bevrnja, called Beni. He was a school comrade of mine. He cursed us, and he cursed our Ustasha mothers, and he said that he would kill all of us if anyone moved. We had our hands behind our heads for about half an hour, and then he allowed us to keep our hands by our sides, and we had to remain standing for about two hours. He then allowed us to sit in a crouching position, and that is the position we remained in until the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This individual called Nijaz - and unfortunately his name is not yet on the transcript. Can you please tell us again the family name of this individual, Nijaz.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Bevrnja, B-e-v-r-n-j-a.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his position at the time?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: He was one of the main commanders in the 307th Brigade Military Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his position within the detention facility Mahmut Busatlija school?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: He only appeared that evening. I only saw him briefly afterwards. I even asked him on one occasion for him to give me a book so that I could have something to read. He didn't even exchange a word with me. He was from the command of the military police in the Mahmut Busatlija school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulic, I'm going to show you now one photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: With the permission of the Trial Chamber. It's actually Prosecution Exhibit P58. Since it has already been tendered, I would like to use the Sanction technology only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulic, please have a look at the photograph in front of you on the screen. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what you can see on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: That's the Mahmut Busatlija grammar school in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the building in whose sports hall you were detained?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, although from this viewpoint, you can't see the hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For the transcript, the witness Tomislav Mikulic identifies the building shown on the photograph Prosecution Exhibit P58 as the gymnasia school building in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulic, I'm going to show you, with the permission of the Trial Chamber, a further photograph. This photograph has already been tendered in the past. It has, however, been tendered under seal. Therefore, the Prosecution provides the hard copies again. Mr. Mikulic, can you please, once you receive the hard copy and once the photograph appears on the screen, can you please have a look, a close look, at the photograph, and can you please afterwards inform the Trial Chamber what you can see on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: This is the sports hall in the Mahmut Busatlija grammar school. As a pupil who attended secondary school, I practiced sports in this sports hall for about two years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the sports hall of the Mahmut Busatlija school you were detained in?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the hall in which I was detained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long, Mr. Mikulic, were you detained in the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: We remained in the sports hall from the 25th of July to the 1st of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are saying "we." How many other people were detained in this sports hall?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: There were about 60 of us in the sports hall itself, between 55 and 60 of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the between 55 and 60, were they all HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I wish to tender this photograph into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have an exhibit number for the photograph of the sports hall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Withopf, perhaps the witness should make a note of his name and authenticate the document. Witness, could you write down your name on the document you'll be presented with, your first and last names, and make a note of today's date too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it the 18th today?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Today is the 17th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 17th of March. Mr. Registrar, an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be P94.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst you were detained in the elementary school, the gymnasia school building - sorry - were you guarded?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Over the day, there would be two soldiers, and in the evening there would usually be three of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the soldiers who guarded you, which army did they form part of?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: They were members of the BH army, of the 307th Brigade and of the military police. I said that that was the command of the military police of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you get to know, Mr. Mikulic, that it was the 307th Brigade and the military police of this brigade?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, I was already aware of the fact that the command was there, because one was free to circulate in the town. One only had to fear the shells that arrived from Serbian positions. So it really wasn't a problem to know this. The members of the Bosniak people knew where the HVO units were located, and likewise, we knew where the BH army units were located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The guards in the gymnasia school building, did they have any military insignia on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: They had the patches of the 307th Brigade on them, and naturally, members of the military police had an additional patch which showed that they were military policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Patches you are referring to, did they actually say "307th Brigade"?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst you were detained in the gymnasia school building, did you become aware of any beatings?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: I saw people who had been beaten, but I didn't see how they were beaten. I saw them leaving and I saw them returning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people who were beaten, were they detainees, as you had been a detainee?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were together from the 25th onwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber about the names of the people, of the detainees who were beaten.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: I don't remember one of the persons' names, but the other two, one of them was a former goal man of the Iskra Dynamo Football Club, Josip Skaro, and the other one was called Dragan Subasic. Josip Skaro, his back was entirely black. It was black and blue as a result of the beatings, and his legs and his face were in a similar state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did one of them, Mr. Mikulic, inform you who beat him?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Josip Skaro said that he recognised one among them, but Nijaz Bevrnja didn't beat him. We heard the sound of beatings. We heard chairs being moved, because that was in one of the adjacent classrooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you yourself beaten?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst you were detained in the gymnasia school building, did you become aware of any other detention facility within the same building whilst you were detained?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, in the area in between -- you enter it from the hall and from the corridor in the grammar school -- we could see members of the MUP, of the military police, and the soldiers who had been captured in their flats. Because in that area -- we passed through that area to reach the toilets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your detention in the gymnasia school building, where were you brought to, if anywhere?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of August, we were put onto a lorry that was used to transport explosives by the former company called Slavko Rodic, which is where I worked too, and I tested shells and detonators, so I knew what the purpose of the vehicle was, because I personally carried out tests in training grounds that the JNA had. Senad Sijamija was the driver and he was also the driver of that lorry in the Slavko Rodic company, in the part called OKP. So this part had to do with testing the quality of the products. We were shoved into this lorry, which was full, completely full, and the distance between the grammar school and the furniture store is about 500 metres. It took us an hour and a half to cover that distance. Many were already feeling sick because we were standing up, and some couldn't hold on to anything, didn't have anything to hold onto.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who, Mr. Mikulic, put you and the others onto that lorry?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Members of the military police put us on the lorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many of you were put on the lorry?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: All of the people who were in the sports hall were driven to the furniture salon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you arrived at the furniture salon, where were you brought to?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: We passed through the ground floor. I think many of the windows had been broken as a result of the shells. So we were taken to the basement, in which there were no windows. The situation there was terrible. The sewer system had broken up, so there were about 15 or 20 centimetres of a mixture of water and urine, excrement. The stench was terrible, and it was very stifling. There was some sort of canisters containing distilled water down there. There was some school benches and some people managed to sit down on these benches or lie down on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, how many people were detained in the basement of the Slavonija furniture salon?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: As I said, it was dark, but I know that we saw members of the military police down there, some MUP members, and others who had been captured in their flats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The military police members and the MUP members you are referring to in your answer, were they Croats?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you guarded whilst detained in the basement of the Slavonija furniture salon?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: The guards were on the ground floor above us, because it wasn't possible for us to leave the basement itself without passing by the guards. So it wasn't necessary for them to be with us. They were above us, on the floor above, and there were members of the military police who were present. I know that a sergeant in the military police was there, Mr. Enes Sijamija was his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The members of the military police, including Mr. Enes Sijamija, which army did he and the other members of the military police form part of?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: They were members of the BH army. I'm not aware of there being any other brigades in Bugojno other than the 307th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the benefit of the Trial Chamber the living conditions in the basement of the Slavonija furniture salon.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: As I said, there was between 15 and 20 centimetres of excrement and water. I've mentioned the living conditions. There was no light. There wasn't sufficient air, just the air that we managed to get from the stairway, but it was very terrible. It was terrible and it was difficult to breathe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long were you and the others detained in the basement of the Slavonija furniture salon?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: We left the furniture salon the same day, this group and myself, and we were transported to the Vojin Paleksic primary school, which is by the former Iskra stadium.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who transported you to the Vojin Paleksic school?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: We went to the Vojin Paleksic school on foot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you volunteer to go to the Vojin Paleksic school?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: No one volunteered. You did what you were ordered to do at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who, if anybody, did escort you from the Slavonija furniture salon to the Vojin Paleksic school?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Naturally, we were escorted by the military police. They escorted us to the Vojin Paleksic school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is the Vojin Paleksic school away from the Slavonija furniture salon?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: I think that the distance is up to about a kilometre and a half, no more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you detained in the Vojin Paleksic school?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: We were detained in the Vojin Paleksic school for about 15 days, 18 days at the most, but I'd say that it was for about 15 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which area of the Vojin Paleksic school were you detained?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: We were detained in the sports hall in the Vojin Paleksic school. The size of this hall was normal. It was quite light. There was parquet floor. It was warm in the hall. We weren't cold. There was enough air. And as it was summer, the floor wasn't cold either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many of you were detained in the Vojin Paleksic school?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: I think there were about 240 or 250 of us on those first few days, on the first two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These 240 or 250, were they all soldiers or were there civilians amongst the detainees?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Perhaps there were a few civilians, but most of them were soldiers who had been captured in the units or in their houses and flats. Some had been captured as civilians, as they had not participated in the fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Amongst the civilians, were there also younger people?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: There were two young boys, 16 years old. They were exchanged on the 19th of March, 1994. And there was an old man who was about 70 or 75 years old. I think he was 75.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please, for the information of the Trial Chamber, describe the living conditions in the Vojin Paleksic school in terms of food, hygiene, and the daily routine.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: The water supply was a problem throughout the town during that period. There was very little water. And among the detainees, five or six lucky men had a few canisters with water or a plastic bottle containing a litre or a litre and a half of juice. As I said, we were allowed to have water.
