It's not that they prevented us from having water, but there really wasn't enough water. So what they managed to obtain during the night is what they would drink. They would give water to those they could give water to. There wasn't enough for everyone. We relieved ourselves in the school toilets. As I said, there was quite a lot of light and it was quite warm, because it was summer. As far as the food itself was concerned, there wasn't enough food. It only arrived on the following day. And for 250 of us, there were six loaves of bread. And a military mess kit - that's what they called it - some cooked food, arrived, but the cooked food that each person received wasn't more than 100 or 150 milliliters. In the Vojin Paleksic school, the representatives of the Bosniak authorities also organised investigations, questionings, conducted by the judge. I personally was questioned by Mesud Duvnjak. Later I found out from a relative of my wife's he was the deputy chief of police in Kupres, that Mesud Duvnjak was an SDA leader in Bugojno and that Dzevad Mlaco was only one of the prominent players. I have to say that Mr. Duvnjak treated me quite fairly, in spite of the minor provocations in the course of the questioning. A record was compiled. They made a note of what I actually said, and that is what I signed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulic, during your detention in the gymnasia school building, in the Slavonija furniture salon, and in the Vojin Paleksic school, did you lose weight?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: It was a short period, so I couldn't have lost much weight during that period, perhaps six or seven kilos. I don't know. You can't lose much weight in ten days' time. But on the 1st of August, when I was taken away to carry out work, that's when I was transferred to the furniture salon, and they asked for ten volunteers to help them unload medical supplies for the hospital. The hospital was about a minute on foot from the furniture salon, but when we got out of the furniture showroom we were put into a van. We knew that we weren't going to the hospital. Because, as I said, they wouldn't have put us in a van to drive us 100 or 150 metres away. They took us to the village of Crnice and took us to the Muslim cemetery. We saw that there were a number of graves that had just -- that were freshly dug. They had just started digging some graves. And some victims had already been buried, victims from the village of Vrbanja. And we were supposed to dig about six or seven graves. I can't remember the exact number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time period you were taken out, were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: When we were taken out, we were not beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you subjected to any other mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: In the furniture showroom, no. Physical harassment, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean, Mr. Mikulic, during the time you were outside the detention, the detention unit and whilst you were digging graves.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: When we had dug out these graves, Velagic, a member of the military police - I know his father's name was Fehko and he had a coffee bar in the Vrbanja neighbourhood - he selected me, Zeljko Milos, Franjo Ribic and Bosko Djerek to go with him to the village of Vrbanja, an area known as Zeleni Put, or green park. We started off on foot through the fields, a poor path that only -- that could only be used by horse-drawn carriages. All the time, Velagic was hitting us, mostly at the back of the head and on our shoulders, with a police truncheon. We were brought to this area of Vrbanja known as Zeleni Put and we were meant to carry out Bosniak victims from a house that had been collected there. Now, whether they were all from the village of Vrbanja, I don't know. As it was very hot, and the victims had been there for several days, one could already see that they had started to decompose, and there were worms coming out of the bodies, and the bodies were wrapped in nylon. We carried, two of us per victim, and put them on the trailer of a small TAM van. And as we carried the dead people, another Velagic, known as Muhko, who was a cousin of the one who had escorted us there, he also beat us all the time with a police baton, on the head and on the back. And after we had loaded four corpses onto the truck, we were supposed to wait for the van to take the victims to the cemetery and then to come back again. In the meantime, Muhko Velagic - which is a nickname, actually, used usually for people whose first name is Muhamed or Muharem - he beat us all the time, on the head, the shoulders, and the kidney area. When he was too tired to continue beating us, he forced us to pick up a police baton, one by one, and to beat one another with it. While he beat us, we had to lie on a slanting path on which broken glass had been thrown from the houses, and we lay there, both face down and back down, looking up at the sun, while he beat us. People had gathered round. Some people were mourning their dead. Some were cursing and insulting us. I recognised Reuf Hadzibegovic, a gynaecologist, a doctor. He was a man of prestige, but he never tried to appease his compatriots, though it is difficult to do that under those circumstances. Some of them would pick up a stone and throw it at us. When we had loaded all the dead onto the truck, Mr. Velagic appeared to have suddenly changed his mind. He allowed us to drink as much water as we wanted and to wash ourselves. We returned to Crnice, where the cemetery was, to a different -- in a different area from the area where we had dug the graves, in the area of what we call Zarasla Medza [phoen], where there were some bushes, two to three metres high. There were ten or so soldiers of the BH army. They weren't there officially. I don't know how they happened to be there. Myself and Zdravko Juricic, who was a math teacher before the war, and for a while he was the principal of an elementary school in Bugojno, and the other group consisted of Zeljko Milos, Zeljko Buljac [phoen], and Frano Ribic. And we were supposed to deepen two graves, as they hadn't been dug deep enough. The soldiers of the BH army provoked us and insulted us there. One of them was standing wearing a completely new camouflage uniform, and from time to time he would throw a stone the size of a fist. And a couple of those hit me in the forehead and cut my head, but it didn't bleed too much. He kept cursing us and insulting us. I didn't know the man, but he knew me. He said: "Look at him, how big the butcher is." And he cursed my Ustasha mother. And Zdravko said that he was an old donkey and that he was the one who had taught us to commit crimes against the Bosniak people. At a certain point in time, I managed to see him pick up a large stone, which was maybe the size of two fists, and he threw it at me. Fortunately, it hit me on the left side of the head, so that I still have a scar in the form of a "Y." My head was cut. Tears started flowing down my face. I was on my knees, like a boxer after he receives many blows in the ring, just about to fall. And the last thing I managed to see was that he picked up a spade and was about to finish me off with the cutting edge of the spade. Luckily, Zdravko reacted quickly and noticed what this one was about to do, and he threw himself over me, and he shouted out: "They're going to kill us." Zdravko got a blow on the elbow, and this soldier picked up a steel bar that we in Bosnia call a "cuskija," and it is used to press the soil and the stones when you're building a fence and pushing pillars into the ground and not into concrete. So you use it to bang the pillar into the ground. And with this pole, he managed to scratch Frano Ribic in the area above his ear. Fortunately, there was no real injury, just a minor scratch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulic, may I please stop you. Do you still today suffer as a result of the severe beatings and all the other forms of mistreatment you just detailed for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: As we left the camp, I had a CT of my head, and it was established that there was some damage at the back of the head where the bones are linked to one another, the cartilage in between the bones. And when the weather changes, I feel pain in the head and my blood pressure goes up and down often. On a number of occasions, my pressure was not -- blood pressure was not more than 60/90 when the doctors took it. From lying on the concrete and as a result of this, I -- my joints hurt, and I always feel cold. I suffer from ischiadicus. But the worst of it is that this is something I shall never be able to fully recover from, because I never have enough sleep. Even after sleep, I don't feel rested. My psychological and physical capacities are considerably reduced in relation to what they were before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulic, from this area where all this mistreatment was inflicted on you, where were you brought to?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: From this cemetery, we were taken back to the furniture showroom again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back, Mr. Mikulic, to the Vojin Paleksic school. I'm going to show you another photograph, with the permission of the Trial Chamber. It's one of the photographs which is already tendered into evidence. It's Prosecution Exhibit P60. And it will be shown via the Sanction technology. Mr. Mikulic, please have a look at the photograph on the screen in front of you. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber what you can see on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: The photograph is of the Vojin Paleksic elementary school in Bugojno, in the neighbourhood Endik [phoen], close to the old Iskra football ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the school you were detained in in 1993?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, the witness identifies the building on Prosecution Exhibit P60, on the photograph of Prosecution Exhibit P60, as the Vojin Paleksic school he was detained. Mr. Mikulic, I'm going to show you another photograph, with the permission of the Trial Chamber, again via Sanction. It's one of the photographs which is already tendered into evidence. It's Prosecution Exhibit P61. Mr. Mikulic, please have a look at the photograph on the screen in front of you. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what this photograph shows.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: This is the gym of the Vojin Paleksic elementary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the gym you and the other detainees were detained in in August 1993?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. I personally slept just below the basket that you can see on the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Again for the sake of the transcript, the witness identifies the sports hall which can be seen on the photograph Prosecution Exhibit P61 as the sports hall of the Vojin Paleksic elementary school he was detained in in August 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the Vojin Paleksic school, where were you brought to?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: From the Vojin Paleksic school, we were taken to the Iskra stadium.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Mikulic, the date, or roughly the date when you were taken to the Iskra stadium?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: I do not recall the exact date, but it was in mid-August, between the 15th and the 18th. So I'm not quite sure which of those two or three days it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are talking about August 1993, don't we?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were all detainees from the Vojin Paleksic school taken to the Iskra stadium?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: The Iskra stadium was the final camp for all of Bugojno's prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is the Iskra stadium from the Vojin Paleksic school?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, the distance, I don't think, is greater than one and a half kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were detained in the Iskra stadium?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: I think that at first, there were more than 400 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the ethnic background of the 400 detainees?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: A soldier whose mother was a Muslim, and there were 14 or 15 soldiers from mixed marriages, Serb/Croat mixed marriages. I think there were two persons of Slovenian extraction. But because they had lived in Bugojno for a long time, they probably declared themselves as Croats. So more than 99 per cent, though the percentage would need to be calculated. I would say more than 97, 98 per cent were Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Detainees, were they all soldiers or were there also civilians amongst them?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: At first there were some civilians as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long were you and the other detainees detained in the Iskra stadium?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: I stayed there until the 19th of March, 1994, when about 300 prisoners who were at the Iskra stadium were all exchanged. I think the final figure was 296.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst you were detained in the Iskra stadium, were you guarded?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Probably a couple of days prior to our arrival at the Iskra stadium, the stadium itself had been rearranged into a real camp. There were observation posts with machine-gun nests, and whenever we were allowed to walk within the compound, the machine-guns were manned by soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were just saying, Mr. Mikulic, a few days prior to your arrival, the Iskra stadium had been rearranged into a real camp. What do you understand under a real camp [sic]?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: The very existence of machine-gun nests and guards with machine-guns guarding us when we walked around reminded me of films with Nazi camps where there were such guards watching over prisoners. We mostly walked with our hands behind our backs. We had to talk very quietly, though we were afraid to do that too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a fence around the Iskra stadium?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: A part of the real wire fence, which can be seen at all football stadiums, existed, but the part that wasn't fenced in, where you enter the changing rooms, and the stadium itself, had reinforced iron netting, and there was a kiosk there, as a kind of entrance point for people entering the camp, and a checkpoint for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The guards in the machine-gun nests, how you describe it, were they soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: They were soldiers and members of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Soldiers and members of the military police of which army?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: The military police of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of which unit?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: I said that, as far as I was familiar with the structure, there was only one brigade of the BH army in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this one brigade was which one?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: The 307th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please, Mr. Mikulic, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, describe the daily routine in the Iskra stadium, including the food conditions, the hygiene conditions.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: In the stadium itself, there was only one toilet, but no running water, and we used it to relieve ourselves. And there was a barrel. We could bring water to that barrel from a nearby small stream, but under soldier escort. And this stream was about 50 metres away from the stadium. Afterwards, three external toilets were made, but we couldn't always use them, but only when the guards would let us. And often, they would not allow us to go even once a day. I personally spent most of the time in a room which was 11 by 6 metres in size, and there were about 140 of us sleeping there. It was very bad. There were some people who had cigarettes and who smoked, so it was smoke-filled and dirty. The floor was covered with wooden pillars with planks on top, wooden beams with planks on top. Several fortunate ones managed to get a blanket from members of the BH army, but a very, very small number. Percentage-wise, probably less than five per cent. The food we received was in very small quantities. We would get six loaves of bread for so many people. One or two, but not full pots of cooked food. Some of the more honourable guards advised some of our people that they knew well not to eat that food, because during the cooking process it had been urinated on. Diarrhoea and stomach problems were widespread. In the evening, they would call out certain names and take people out for beatings. People were taken from the camp to the front lines, where they mostly dug trenches and made shelters for soldiers of the BH army who were there holding positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I just stop you there, Mr. Mikulic. Earlier on you were mentioning that within a few days, you said six to ten days or so, you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. lost six to eight kilogrammes of weight. Whilst you were detained in the Iskra stadium, did you lose additional weight?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: While we had this poor food it was -- well, this lasted up until the end of October. I personally lost over 25 kilos. I was just skin and bone. I couldn't even stand up normally. I was hunched when I walked and I had to hold onto my stomach. Most of us were unfortunate in that -- I, for example, ate three small slices of bread over a ten-day period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did other detainees, Mr. Mikulic, to your knowledge, also lose weight?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: We couldn't weigh ourselves. All we could do was look at each other and see how terrible we looked, see how we walked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A few minutes ago, Mr. Mikulic, you were briefly talking about beatings in the Iskra stadium. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber in some more detail.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: This took place in the evening, once night had fallen. I don't know how the names of soldiers were called out. I don't know who did it. All I know is that someone's name would be called out, the person would be asked to come out. They didn't even take these persons further away to prevent the beating from being heard. They beat them in the vicinity, and we could hear the people groaning. But what I am certain of is that each one of us was able to recognise one of the shift commanders. There was someone called Djopo. He participated in calling out these men, these people, and beating them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, Mr. Mikulic, how often did such beatings happen?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Sometimes it happened every evening, and then that would stop. If high-ranking officials found out about it, military political officials, and then it would happen again. There were no strict rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulic, these beatings, how soon after your arrival in August 1993 in the Iskra stadium, how soon did they become a repeated occurrence?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, these beatings took place, as I have described, and it continued in this way until mid-November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it already start in August?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a repeated occurrence between August 1993 and mid-November 1993?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: As I said, it would happen in this manner for several nights in a row and then it would stop and then it would start again. There were no strict rules. It depended on the guards on shift. I know that when some guards were on shift, these people were good and fair, and we were almost certain on such occasions that no one would be beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there also other guards?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: What do you mean? Other units? Other -- other what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were just saying, Mr. Mikulic, that when some guards were on the shift, these people were good, fair, and, "We were almost certain not to be beaten." Were there also guards who were involved in calling out the people for beatings and were involved in the beatings?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: I said that there was a commander called Djopa, and there was a military policeman. Mustafica was his name. I know his brother very well, as well as his relatives. It was a very good-looking family. I even spent a couple of nights with the brother of that military policeman. I studied with his son. And on that occasion he spoke to me about his brother whom I subsequently met as a military policeman. He said he was a very bad man, that he wasn't serious, that he had caused problems for his parents and told me that he had got married on two occasions, although he was only 22 or 23 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Mikulic, what about this military policeman called Djopo, or Mustafica?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: When Djopo was the shift commander, I think there were eight to ten guards on a shift. On such occasions we were afraid that people would be beaten, and unfortunately that is what frequently happened. Zijad Salkic, who used to be a footballer in Iskra, was on his shift. Sometimes he often defended us and didn't allow people to be beaten. But Salkic threatened him later. Salkic told my relative -- he said that we shouldn't be defended. He defended his best man, Kazimir Kajic, too, who was also an Iskra footballer, and he was also beaten on several occasions. Mustafica, as I have said, some detainees said that he personally beat them when he took them out. But what I can say for certain is that he confiscated items from us, and he even blackmailed some soldiers. He took them home so that they could wash themselves at home, and in order to be able to take some things from them in their houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mikulic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this concludes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. It's more or less time to have the break now. It would be best if we had our break now and commence with the cross-examination at about five to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Mikulic. My name is Edina Residovic. I represent General Hadzihasanovic. I'd like to express my sympathy for the experiences you have been through, but I will have to ask you a number of questions that have to do with the general context and also with the facts that you have already discussed with my learned colleague from the Prosecution. Mr. Mikulic, is it correct to say that you were born in Potkralj in Donji Vakuf municipality but that before the war and in the course of the war itself, up until the time when you were exchanged, you lived in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: I lived in Potkralj, in my parents' home, until 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in 1992, you moved to Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: No. When I went to the unit, I went home on five occasions in that year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war, you worked in the Slavko Rodic company as an engineer; is that correct? I apologise, but your answer hasn't been recorded.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. I worked in the Slavko Rodic company as a technician. I checked the quality of products.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You worked in the military sphere?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. Most of the items produced in the Slavko Rodic company were for the military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although the Trial Chamber is already aware of the position that Bugojno is in in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I only have a number of questions that I would like to ask you, in order to confirm some of the facts that have already been mentioned. Would it be correct to say that Bugojno is in the upper part of the river of Vrbas, in the so-called Skopalj valley; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But when you say "the so-called," it's not a good term, because this is a real geographic location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: You can see this on the maps yourself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That area is between the Vranica and Radusa mountains and it's about 20 kilometres wide and three to eight kilometres long, that valley?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. That would be the size of the valley, from Donji Vakuf to Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you go uphill -- upstream, up the river, in that valley, about 18 kilometres away you have the town of Gornji Vakuf, and downstream, about 12 kilometres lower down, there is Donji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. That would be the distance as the crow flies, more or less. The Vrbas follows a straight line from Gornji Vakuf to Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say, Mr. Mikulic, that in the last ten years, in the ten years preceding the war, Bugojno was very strong economically and before the war broke out it was one of the important industrial centres in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that this period of rapid development started about 1975 or 1976 and continued not until 1999. You know that the crisis in the former Yugoslavia started about 1988. Business wasn't so good in many companies. But during those 12 years, the development in Bugojno was very rapid in comparison to other areas in the BH republic or in other republics of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can certainly confirm that at the very beginning of the war, in 1992, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Serbian forces immediately occupied Donji Vakuf and the mountain pass Komar, so that this route, being the main route to Travnik, Sarajevo, and Zenica, could no longer be used; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The alternative route was the route which was partly a macadam route, and it went through Rostovo, the Rostovo plateau, Novi Travnik and Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. I passed through that pass about two years ago, and before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bugojno could also be connected to Herzegovina, that is to say, to the southern parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You could reach it through Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, and Jablanica too; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the main road, the republican road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This road via Prozor, in 1992 and 1993, was under the control of the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not the entire road. You know the Bosniaks were in the majority at some sections, but on the whole there weren't any conflicts, so the road was open.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that in 1992 you immediately joined the HVO. You did this is in June; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time, in Bugojno, there was a Territorial Defence municipal staff which was a legitimate military structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not join the Territorial Defence; you joined the 2nd Battalion of the Eugen Kvaternik HVO Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although you worked as an official in the headquarters, you were a soldier in the full sense of the term. You wore a uniform and you had been given a weapon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: In March, when one of my Bosniak friends handed over his equipment and his rifle, that is when I was given his rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The brigade headquarters was in Tito's villa on the hill of Gorica, which was one of the most elevated points above the town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your brigade was within the subordination system of the HVO and the main headquarters was in Grude?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: The headquarters was in Grude.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew that at the time the decision had been taken to form the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which included 30 municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This included the municipality of Bugojno; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, according to the decisions of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, HVO units were also formed which were the only armed forces in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: There were certain complications where the population was mixed, and this is why these tragic events occurred among these two -- between these two peoples.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because of the decision of the leadership of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, they did not only form parallel military structures; they also took decisions about forming parallel civil organs of power; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Bosniaks and the Croats had their own structures of power, independent of each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Croats, who had been legally elected to the organs of power at the elections, withdrew and they formed the HVO, which was the civilian organ of power in Bugojno too; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: In Bugojno, the councilmen from the -- the deputies from the HDZ had the majority, and they did what was done in all such environments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, since you occupied the position that you have already mentioned, you knew who the responsible officials and organs were, and you knew who was responsible for certain functions. You knew that the president of the War Presidency in the municipality of Bugojno was Dzevad Mlaco at the time?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew that at the time, in 1992 and 1993, the president of the War Presidency in Bugojno municipality was Dzevad Mlaco; were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the Bosniak part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The president of the HVO, as a civilian organ of power, was Vladimir Soljic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's answer wasn't audible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The War Presidency, the War Presidency of Bugojno in 1992 and 1993 --

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, just a technical issue. The interpreters have made us available [sic] that the witness's answer to one of the questions of my learned colleague wasn't audible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's line 7 on page 63. You should ask the witness the question again. The question concerning Vladimir Soljic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulic, your answer hasn't been entered into the transcript. Would it be correct to say that the president of the HVO as a civilian organ of power in Bugojno was Vladimir Soljic?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1992 and in 1993, the War Presidency in Bugojno had real power over the civilian and military structures, the Bosniak structures in Bugojno; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the very beginning, although the structures existed independently, the HVO command and the Territorial Defence staff tried to agree on forming a joint command, and the first such meeting was held on the 6th of May, 1992. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: In those high-level circles, well, I didn't have any access to those circles. I didn't have access to information. So I couldn't answer your question, either positively or negatively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, you can probably confirm the fact that that joint command, in spite of all the attempts that were made, never actually functioned in Bugojno, never actually came to life.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness nodded.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that in addition to the Territorial Defence and later the BH army and the HVO, there were civilian police units in Bugojno too?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. There's another problem. I said would it be correct to say that this joint command never actually functioned. Your answer hasn't been recorded. So could you please answer whether this is correct.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it never came to life. It never functioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to the HVO, as a military structure, and the BH army, which was also a military structure, and there was the civilian police presence in Bugojno and the reserve civilian police force was present too; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, some of the population fit for military service after a state of war had been declared was mobilised into the reserve police force, and the commander of that special police force was Nijaz Bevrnja. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak up when answering questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In February 1993, in addition to the Eugen Kvaternik brigade, certain Home Guard units in Bugojno were formed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When these -- these units were formed as a result of an order that a general mobilisation of the Croatian population should be carried out, and they were formed on a territorial basis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The commander of the Home Guard battalion in Bugojno was Dragan Erkapic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In response to a question put to you by my learned colleague, you said that at one point in time, some Bosniaks were mobilised into the HVO. Would it be correct to say that the HVO units in 1992 and in 1993 were far better equipped and armed than the BH army units?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: As far as heavy weapons are concerned, I can't tell you anything about that. As far as infantry weapons are concerned, I noticed that BH army members and HVO members had automatic rifles. I can't tell you anything about the artillery, because I was never at BH army or HVO positions. The HVO had better equipment, uniforms, training, winter jackets, et cetera. As far as food supplies are concerned, they had better food supplies. I can tell you about this because I have information about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All these units and the reserve police force, the HVO and the BH army, all the members of these units wore camouflage uniforms, and you could only identify them on the basis of the patches they had on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the whole, you could only identify them on the basis of the patches on their uniforms, although -- well, the camouflage uniforms were rarely different to the ones that the BH army wore and the army wore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that in 1992 a large number of refugees arrived in Bugojno, first of all from Krajina, then from Donji Vakuf, and later on, and after Jajce had fallen, other refugees arrived; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After Jajce had fallen, some Croatian refugees arrived in Bugojno, but most of them did not remain in Bugojno. They moved on to Croatia or to certain other areas where there was no fighting?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Bosniak refugees who arrived without anything mainly remained in the area of Bugojno and, as you have already said, this caused significant demographic changes in the town itself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The demographic structure changed as a result of the fact that many of the local population, especially the Croatian population, women and children, left Bugojno because of the war and went to other areas, so this also had an effect?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could also say that before the conflict itself, in July, there were only seven to eight thousand local Croats in Bugojno. Is this information correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, even less, I would say, because if there were 15.000 Croats in total, then it would be 15.900. I don't know. Many people worked abroad, in Germany and Western Europe. Their families would go to be with them if they managed to do so, and the local inhabitants who were able to go to Western countries at the time went to Croatia, and I think that that figure is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that is that already then numerous refugees moved into abandoned houses in the surroundings of Bugojno and in Bugojno itself?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: People had no choice. They had to live somewhere. They were given certain certificates for temporary accommodation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was just about to ask you about that. You do know that the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina passed regulations on temporary accommodation in temporarily abandoned apartments and properties, and that decisions about accommodation in those facilities were taken by the civilian authorities in Bugojno; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can remember, before the refugees moved in, there were no incidents, as far as I was aware. As far as possible, they were put up in these apartments. Some people were luckier than others. Some entered a destroyed house and had to repair it himself to be able to live in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In answer to a question from my learned friend opposite, you said that within the framework of your duties in the headquarters, you also issued certain certificates. Do you know that also Bosniaks who had to leave Bugojno needed to have HVO's permissions to be able to pass through HVO checkpoints and areas under HVO control?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of this, because the places that one had to go through to go to Croatia and from there further on, were checked by the military police, and I don't think this was an obligation introduced by the HVO of Bugojno but by request of the authorities in Tomislavgrad, Livno, and other towns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Though this obligation existed earlier on, and I'm asking you, do you know that on the 8th of April, 1993, there was a meeting held in Travnik of representatives of the HDZ and the HVO of the entire area of Bosnia, with commanders of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and that at that meeting, the question of leaving towns was addressed, and it was stated that no one could leave without such permits?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you about that. I wasn't a member of any leading body. I was just an ordinary clerk at a very low level. I wasn't linked to the headquarters at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I see. You've corrected me. You were not at the headquarters. You were in the 2nd Battalion. In view of the existence of these checkpoints on the way out of town, you probably knew that already in the spring of 1993, there were minor or major incidents that took place at these checkpoints in and around Bugojno. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All this, plus the fact that in Gornji Vakuf, which is only 18 kilometres from Bugojno, there was continuous fighting between the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Council, resulted in certain tensions in the town of Bugojno itself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, quite, obviously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that on the 9th of May, 1993, the HVO captured 38 members of the army at the Humac checkpoint; after that, the army, in the night between the 9th and 10th, captured a group of 20 HVO members; then again the HVO captured seven army members, which further aggravated the existing tensions in town?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: I can't speak about the numbers you are referring to, because I had no official reports. But it is a fact that these incidents occurred and aggravated the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I notice several times that my learned friend from the Defence puts, quite often, two, three, or four different facts into one question. That appears to be a bit problematic. I would therefore suggest that my learned friend phrases her questions differently and only puts one fact in one question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is the case. On page 68, line 8, where there are several points in the question. So, for the clarity of the hearing, it would be better for you to ask one question at a time. It's much clearer, and it is clearer for the witness too, who doesn't have to confront a host of questions within a single question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, and I will do as you suggest. And I think indeed that that would be a better course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even though my question was complicated, you did give an answer. Because you were not familiar with the figures, but you were aware of those incidents?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also knew that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HVO were endeavouring to overcome these excess situations?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Both sides in those days, the commanders, both Lucic and Granic, were doing their best to avoid any conflicts, and if they had the main say, there would have been no conflicts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, in view of the position you held in the battalion of which you were a member, you certainly know that on the 17th of July in the village of Vrbanja, at a crossroads leading to the village of Kandija, the HVO established a checkpoint and that immediately after that the locals of Vrbanja formed a separate checkpoint. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that they were locals. I think they were members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the village of Vrbanja set up another checkpoint 500 metres away. At that checkpoint, there was an armed clash in which members of the army killed members of the HVO anti-terrorist group, that is, Miroslav Telenta, and later Mijo Vucak was killed as well. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Our information was that they were killed almost simultaneously, that Mijo Vucak was taken into a stable and killed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that on that same day, in order to investigate the causes of the death of these two HVO soldiers, a joint mixed commission was set up, consisting of four MUP members of Bosnia and Herzegovina and four MUP members of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that, but I learnt, while a captive in the grammar school, that this group had carried out an on-site investigation and that two Bosniak policemen were killed. I knew one of them personally. He was from a village close by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This killing and the HVO attack marked the beginning of the conflict in Bugojno, which spread from the village of Vrbanja to the whole town; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: That week, there was tension. I know that some of our members were captured and taken to the grammar school immediately. But the actual armed conflict -- this was on Sunday. But the actual armed conflict started on Monday, early in the morning, 4.00 or 5.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that point in time, as you said repeatedly, there was only one brigade of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that is the 307th Brigade in Bugojno, and there was one HVO brigade, the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade, and the Home Guard Battalion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you had heard about this incident in which two members of the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina were killed as well, you certainly know that in attacking Vrbanja, the HVO killed 54 Bosniak civilians, that the village was set on fire and totally destroyed?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: I do know that on the 1st of August, when I was at the cemetery in Crnice and I heard from the Islamic priest whom I knew by sight, because he was from the village of Porica, and when he was talking to some elderly people, whether they were from Crnice or Vrbanja, I don't know, that the victims from Vrbanja had been buried and that the total number was 19 victims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In answer to a question from the Prosecutor you said, and you have now repeated that you were taken to do work in town, in this specific case to dig graves, I'm asking you whether you know that for work in town that was done up until the end of 1993 the person -- the body responsible was the civilian authority of Bugojno municipality?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Probably the civilian authority because I saw some doctors of ours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The last question of my learned colleague appears to be problematic in light of the Trial Chamber's decision of 16th of March, 2004. Forced labour, pursuant to this decision, is not an issue either of the parties can lead evidence. I therefore oppose against such sort of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The decision rendered excluded formally from the Indictment all reference to inhumane treatment and forced labour, but I didn't think that you intended to embark upon that question, because it was upon your request that we dealt with that problem. Your question must have a different connotation. Could you respond to this particular point raised.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we received your decision today and we're familiar with its contents. I am limiting myself to the examination-in-chief of the Prosecutor who kept asking the witness about what was happening outside the prison in which he was held, and secondly what I want to ask the witness about is the chain of command in view of the fact that the witness, during the examination-in-chief testified about everything that happened at the cemetery at Vrbanja and Crnice, but my aim is not to continue along those lines, but to establish certain chains of command and questions of subordination in Bugojno itself. And since the witness has answered my question, I should like to ask him to look at a document, which we will propose to be marked for identification only, so that I may go on to my next question. Could this document please be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Put the question to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulic, you see this document. I know that you have not had occasion to see it before, but my question would be: Is it true that the War Presidency of Bugojno municipality was the civilian organ of authority in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: The War Presidency was probably both a civilian and military organ Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of authority in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Executive Board was actually the government of Bugojno at the time, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: You're asking me things about which I couldn't say, because I wasn't present there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the role of Zair Mijo [phoen] in Bugojno was at the time?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: I think he was the president. I knew Zair Mujo [phoen] while he worked in TBM. I know that he was a very fine man. Now, what he did during the war, I don't know. I know that he was chief of some sort, but of what, I don't know. I can't help you there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in view of the fact that this is a relevant document, and we can't expect the witness to be able to authenticate this document, we would like it to be marked for identification, and could it be given a number then, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask you something? What is the purpose of producing this document and showing it to me? Do you wish to prove that we, as prisoners, were not working in town, were not digging trenches on the front lines? I don't know what the meaning of this document is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I never called in question what you testified about. I have already explained that in the chain of command, as the Defence team, we are establishing various facts, including the fact regarding the labour done in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: I saw these work labour teams. My friends, Croats, engineers and doctors, who were cleaning streets.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have a number for this document, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, what is your position regarding this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, if it's only for the purpose of marking for identification for the time being, the Prosecution doesn't oppose the marking for identification. However, my learned colleague could please inform the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution about the source of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is what we noted each time. What is the source of this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the investigation, during the pre-trial period, our investigators reviewed the archives in Bugojno municipality, and this document, and another document that I will be showing the witness, are from the archives in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, give us a number for the B/C/S and for the English versions of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the B/C/S document gets Exhibit number DH62, marked for identification; and the English translation gets the Exhibit number DH62/E, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulic, I only have a couple of more questions for you. Is it true that before the war, there was no prison in Bugojno except for some sort of a detention area attached to the police itself?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: I do know that the HVO formed a prison in the elementary school in Gracanica, where Serbs were imprisoned, but very small numbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe we didn't understand one another properly. My question was: Before the war, there was no prison in Bugojno, is that right, prisoners went to the KP Dom in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Bugojno did not have a prison, at least as far back as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In answer to a question from my learned friend the Prosecutor, you said that you came to the Iskra stadium in the second half of August and that the stadium was a unified prison for all HVO prisoners; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before that, all the locations in which you and others were detained were actually temporary places of detention; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, probably, since we didn't spend any length of time there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now like to ask the next and last document that I intend to show this witness to be shown to the witness. We have a sufficient number of copies for Their Honours and my learned friends. Before you have a look at this document, do you know someone called Mehmed Sadikovic?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: I think the gentleman who worked in a construction firm, Gorica Bugojno, had such a name. I think he was a manager there, because that's what the detainees who worked in Gorica said. They said that he was a colleague of theirs, and he was a commander in prison while we were in the Vojin Paleksic school. I know this for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Have a look at the document now. This document, as it states, is a decision on appointing a warden of temporary detention facilities in Bugojno; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document was issued by Bugojno municipality, by the War Presidency, an organ which, as you have said, also performed both civilian duties and military duties, had both civilian and military authority?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, given the importance of the document and its contents, given the fact that it is closely related to all the counts in the indictment that concern Bugojno, and given that the witness has confirmed that he is aware of the fact that the person mentioned in this decision was the prison warden, I suggest that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask you a question? Unfortunately, we weren't detainees. We were slaves. Detainees are given certain sentences. They are questioned. They have certain security. We had no such things. Unfortunately, many of my friends lost their lives. They were killed in the most brutal way. And I don't think that this is something that is done in prisons. And I believe that the person who compiled this document didn't order that we should be eliminated, but that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have already said, I am very sorry for all the experiences you have had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Before Mr. Withopf takes the floor to comment on the second document, the Trial Chamber notes a number of factors, a number of things. First of all, the second document was compiled on the 28th of July. The president of the war municipality was Mr. Dzevad Mlaco. And the second document was on the 24th of September, 1993. That's the date. And the president apparently changed, because it's Mr. Zaid Nevo [phoen]. The second thing I'd like to point out is that these two documents refer to another document. It refers to guidelines. The second one refers to Article 9 and 10, and the first one to Article 3. But in the first document provided, the first document was delivered to the commander of the 307th Mechanised Brigade, whereas the second document doesn't mention any addressee. In the second document, it doesn't state that this document will be published in the Official Gazette of Bugojno municipality, which was the case for the first document. If the documents seem to agree as far as the form is concerned, there are certain differences as far as the substance is concerned, in particular with regard to the list of people to which it was forwarded. These are the comments I wanted to make before hearing the Defence's [as interpreted] position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution has the very same concerns about this document as you, Mr. President, just expressed. In addition, the Prosecution objects against tendering this document into evidence for a number of additional reasons. The witness was not able to comment on this document to any extent beyond the actual contents of the document. The document refers to the temporary prison, and I really emphasise it's the singular only, whereas my learned friend in her questions used the word -- used the description "temporary prisons," in the plural. I really wish to emphasise that. And the third reason why the Prosecution objects to tender this document into evidence: The Prosecution can see the relevance of this document. It doesn't say anything about what prison is referenced to in the document. Nobody knows whether one of the six detention facilities in Bugojno is actually covered by this document. For the reasons you, Mr. President, just expressed, and for the additional reasons I just detailed, the Prosecution objects against tendering this document into evidence, and it would also object against marking this document for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we have marked the first document for identification, we'll do the same for the second document, and the Trial Chamber will then deliberate to see what we'll do with the documents. Is there anything else the Defence would like to add?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to respond to a number of issues that you have raised. In fact, the second document that I have produced - it's an early one; it's dated the 28th of July, 1993 - was issued by the War Presidency, which functions as the Municipal Assembly in wartime conditions and was signed by the president, Dzevad Mlaco. In response to my questions, the witness said he knew who the president of the War Presidency was in 1992 and 1993, and this has been entered into the transcript. The second document was issued by the Executive Board of the War Presidency. In our conditions, this is the government. It's not the Municipal Assembly; it's the government. These two organs are different organs, and as a result, the references, the headings, can be different, the ones that you have mentioned. Secondly, as far as the persons to whom the documents were forwarded, I think that each organ decides whom its decisions should be forwarded to. And the War Presidency, in the document dated the 28th of July, 1993, stated that this decision on appointing someone, because this is a specific act, should enter into force immediately. Since this is a specific act, it's not a decision that establishes an organ, and as a result, it's not necessary to have this published in an official gazette. That concerns the form. As far as the substance is concerned, I think that I have already indicated what the importance of the document is. And secondly, the witness, in response to a question that I put to him, and it only concerned the name of Mehmed Sadikovic, the witness clearly said that he was aware of the fact that he was the prison warden when he was being held in one of the detention facilities. I no longer know whether it was in the grammar school or in the furniture showroom, but it has most certainly been recorded in the transcript as one of the witness's answers. As a result, I think that this document is important, and the position [as interpreted] stands by its request to have this admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will mark this document for identification and we'll deliberate on the matter subsequently. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the B/C/S version gets Exhibit number DH63, marked for identification; and the English translation gets Exhibit number DH63/E, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. Mikulic, thank you. I have no further questions. Thank you for having answered my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does the other Defence team have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we don't have any questions. Mr. Kubura is not charged with any of the alleged incidents that this witness has testified about today. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dixon. Mr. Withopf, do you have any further questions, given that we have another ten minutes now?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution has no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This concludes your testimony. You have answered the questions put to you by the Prosecution and by the Defence. The Defence took care to tell you that in spite of the unpleasant experiences you have had, they had to perform their duties as a Defence team. Thank you for having come to testify at The Hague, and we wish you a good trip home. I'll now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a few more minutes. I would like to ask the Defence about the model. What stage are we at? You said, last time that we spoke about this, that you were examining the issue, and I was expecting to see it very rapidly. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'll be glad to offer you some explanations about the subject. First of all, I would like to take this opportunity to thank the Registrar. They have made this task of transporting the model to the Tribunal easy. It is now near -- in a room near the courtroom and it's ready to be used. We were to use it for the witness who was withdrawn last week. This was, in our opinion, the best witness for providing certain explanations to the Trial Chamber in connection with the model. As soon as another witness appears who might be able to make good use of the model, we will use the model, when such a witness appears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your explanations, Mr. Bourgon. I'll now turn to Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, as I said repeatedly, the Prosecution, on principle, does not object using such a model. However, prior to using it, the Prosecution wishes to have a number of issues addressed and a number of answers -- of questions answered by the Defence. It would be beneficial for the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution to get to know who is the originator of this model, when was it created, for what purpose was it created, and what is actually the scale of the model. Once the Prosecution has an opportunity to see the model, there may be other issues the Prosecution wishes to raise. Therefore, we reserve our right to make additional comments and to ask additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have already informed our colleagues from the Prosecution about certain matters and we can also provide you with additional information. The model was made by the BH Army of the Federation, and we submitted a request to the Army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina to provide us with such a model so that we could use it in the course of the proceedings. And if the Trial Chamber could consider that this model could be used as evidence, we asked them to make this model available to us. The Federation army said that they would make this available, and we then informed the Trial Chamber that we might perhaps manage to obtain a model of the area in question. I would also like to say that professional persons from the Federation army probably made the model. I don't know the exact dimensions. My colleagues have just told me that the scale is 50.000. This is just a geographic depiction of the area. I also have to say that that model existed in the Federation army far earlier. But part of the model was made available for the Blaskic case, either to the Prosecution or to the Defence - I don't know to whom at the moment - and it was used in the case, and as a result, that part of the model was modified. So the technical execution is somewhat different, although the model is identical. Mr. President, we are in a -- we wouldn't want to address all issues before the Trial Chamber. As the model is in the building, we can show the model to the Prosecution, and if they have any additional questions, we can answer them. But we think that the arrival of international witnesses might be the right time for using that model. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. At the moment, at this stage, I think that the best solution would be for the Prosecution to examine the model with the Defence, if the model is in the building. If it were miles away, that would be a problem, but it is here. So, Mr. Withopf, I'm sure you will be able to find a few minutes to examine the model. So try to arrange this with Defence, and you will then be able to examine the entire model, and then you can inform us of whether there are any problems or not. But this is a model made by the army. The scale is 1:50.000. It's a model of a geographic area, and I don't see why this should be problematic. Perhaps there might be a problem, but in order to discover any problems, you should first see the model. The best course of action would be for you to examine the model and then inform us of your opinion of the model after you have seen it, and this can be done within the context of exchanging documents between the parties. Mr. Withopf, you may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this is exactly along the lines what would have been the suggestion by the Prosecution. I would, however, be very grateful to my learned friends from the Defence if they could inform the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution which section of the army made the model and for what purpose it has been made, for what military purpose. There may lie a problem, but I'm sure my learned friends from the Defence can answer such questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Prosecution would like to know which branch or unit of the BH army made the model. And the second question was what was the purpose of the model. But it appears that you have already answered that, because you said that part of the model was already used in another case before the Tribunal, and I assume that the purpose was the same. But perhaps you could now answer the questions raised by Prosecution. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. At this stage, the information we can provide the Trial Chamber is that in most armies, there are models of territory where an army is supposed to take action, and very often one prepares models, makes models, and it's the model department of the army in question that actually makes these models. These models are made to make it possible to examine the territory, so that the officers may be aware of the territory that they might have to act in. In the case of this model, as I have already informed the Trial Chamber, this is part of a model which is far bigger. It's almost as large as this room, and it represents the entire area of Bosnia. We have managed to obtain part of this model; that is to say, we have managed to obtain the area referred to in the indictment. So, Mr. President, there's nothing secret. I'm sure that when my colleague sees the model, he'll realise that it's only a visual aid, an aid that should make it possible for all the parties to have a better idea of the lay of the land. And the most interesting thing is the relief, the possibility of seeing the mountains and realising what the distance between the towns is. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, the best thing would be for you to see the model itself, and then the Trial Chamber will be all ears when it comes to you expressing your position with regard to the model. It's now 7.00. We will now adjourn, and I would like to invite everyone to appear for the hearing that will start tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 18th day of March, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25
